A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Cybench and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original tasks, experiments, and example logs can be matched across relocation and renumbering, supporting reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of eight language models on 40 cybersecurity tasks, including aggregate results in Table 2, per-task results in Tables 4–6, and agent logs.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds scaffold comparisons, repeated-attempt evaluations, memory-budget experiments, and analyses of submissions, refusals, and resource usage.

M1.justification: v2 uses one structured bash agent. v3 adds action-only responses, continuous pseudoterminal interaction, and a web-search tool as alternative scaffolds (Section 5 and Appendix A). These change response generation or available actions; the original agent is retained under the structured bash name.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 40 tasks from four competitions across six cybersecurity categories. The new experiments reuse these tasks and their subtasks. Scaffold and memory changes alter evaluation procedures, not dataset or task coverage; v2 already permitted network access.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 adds direct comparisons between structured bash, action-only, pseudoterminal, and web-search agents for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o. These substantially expand the evaluated comparison methods. The original eight-model comparison remains unchanged; the cited AISI evaluation is external discussion, not a newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: v3 adds best-of-three scaffold evaluations and a separate full-history experiment with 128K input tokens for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 126K for GPT-4o. Appendices B–C add submission-based and log2(FST)-weighted metrics. The original iteration limits and token budgets are retained for the original experiment.

E4.justification: v3 adds scaffold ablations and case studies examining interpretation failures, terminal interaction, and search use (Appendix A), submission-rate analysis (B), difficulty-weighting analysis (C), and a memory-budget experiment (I). Appendix N also expands refusal analysis. These investigate important questions absent from v2's analyses.

E5.justification: v3 explicitly identifies the original results as single-attempt and specifies three attempts with maximum-performance aggregation for the added scaffold experiments. Usage tables report medians across those attempts. This adds replication and aggregation information, but neither version reports confidence intervals, seed-based variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 scores and corresponding per-task performance entries are retained. New best-of-three results include Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieving 27.5% subtask-guided success with pseudoterminal versus 17.5% with structured bash (v3 Table 3); these are new experimental conditions, not same-setting gains over v2. v3 also adds memory, weighted-score, submission, and usage results, expands refusals to Sonnet, and changes Opus's Delulu subtask label from Attempted to Refusal.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces the mathematical weighting rule log2(FST) for new difficulty-weighted performance measures. The act–execute–update equations and formal environment definitions are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantial theoretical derivation is added.

C1.justification: The central claims about the benchmark, subtasks, professional-level tasks, and unguided difficulty ceiling remain. v3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the evaluation contribution from one agent scaffold to four and add the finding that scaffold effects depend on the model.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving action-space expressivity versus complexity and GPT-4o's lower answer-submission rate. New limitations acknowledge that the scaffolds are far from the capability frontier and that CTFs emphasize short tasks, small codebases, and constructed vulnerabilities. It also qualifies the single-attempt memory experiment and comparisons with externally reported AISI results.

D1.justification: v3 supplies prompts and interaction examples for the new scaffolds, clarifies that observation parsing credits flags rather than intermediate subtask answers, and adds extensive token, runtime, and iteration reporting in Appendix L. Existing model identifiers move to Appendix J, and the original prompt and public code/data access statement are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to 3CB, work on reporting train-test overlap, and the joint US/UK AISI evaluation, while removing the chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought references. It extends its positioning to claim first use of Kali Linux, web search, and pseudoterminal access for CTF agents. Most related-work coverage remains.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 standardizes FST and structured bash terminology, streamlines related-work descriptions, revises Section 5's organization, moves model details into an appendix, and reorganizes the appendices around the added analyses. Author order and contribution statements also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds three prompt figures with highlighted additions and deletions, colored scaffold-comparison tables, submission and weighted-score tables, and extensive performance and usage matrices. The refusal table gains model/scaffold information and expands across pages. Existing overview diagrams, difficulty plots, and original result tables are largely retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: v2's capability assessment depended on one scaffold. v3 substantially strengthens it through scaffold comparisons, failure analyses, a memory-budget experiment, and explicit limits on generalization (Table 3 and Appendices A–C and I). Prompt and resource reporting also improve reproducibility. Best-of-three results still lack uncertainty estimates, and the broad scaffold-effect claims need qualification across metrics, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and interpretation.
